name: Baloot
description: Baloot is the quintessential card game of Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, a high-strategy trick-taking contest derived from the French Belote. Played by four players in partnerships, it revolves around two primary contracts: 'Sun' (No-Trump) and 'Hokom' (Trump). The game is famous for its complex card values that shift based on the contract, and for 'Projects'â€”valued combinations like sequences and four-of-a-kinds. It is not just a game but a cultural institution, demanding intense concentration and partnership signaling.

history.origins: Brought to the Arabian Peninsula by French influence or via merchants in the early 20th century. While it shares the DNA of Belote, it was heavily adapted to local tastes, particularly with the introduction of the 'Sun' contract and the doubling of scores.
timeline: 1920s: Belote-style games appear in Hijaz (Western Saudi Arabia).
1950s: Rules for 'Sun' and 'Hokom' stabilize into the modern Baloot format.
2018: The first officially sanctioned Saudi Baloot Championship is held in Riyadh with a record-breaking prize pool.
Present: One of the most played social games in the Arab world, with numerous high-quality mobile apps.
history.cultural: Typically played in 'Siraus' (social gatherings) where tea and conversation accompany the rigorous mental play.
history.evolution: Modern Baloot has become highly standardized due to national tournaments, which settled many regional rule disputes.

setup.deck: 32-card pack. Remove cards 2-6 from a standard 52-card deck.
setup.dealing: Dealer gives 3 cards to each player, then 2. The next card is turned face up. Players then bid to take the contract (Hokom/Sun or Pass). Once a contract is chosen, the dealer finishes the deal so everyone has 8 cards.

rules.objective: The first team to reach 152 points wins. Points are earned from card values in tricks, the final trick bonus, and declared 'Projects'.
rules.gameplay: Players must follow suit. If unable to follow in Hokom, you must play a trump card. The winner of the trick leads the next.
keyRules: Last Trick: The final trick provides an extra 10 points (called 'Abna'a').
Card Points: Total card points in Sun = 130; in Hokom = 162.
The 'Gawa': A specialized verbal challenge to double the score.

strategy.basic: In Hokom, lead your trumps early to exhaust the opponents' ability to ruff your winning Kings and Aces. In Sun, focus on establishing control through long suits.
strategy.intermediate: Watch the discards. If your partner discards a 7 of Spades, they are likely signals that they have no more Spades. Use this to lead Spades and let them trump in.
strategy.advanced: The 'Lock' (Qafel): If you have the best trumps, you can 'lock' the game, meaning trumps cannot be led. This allows you to walk through with your long suit and wipe out the contractor.
tips: Always declare your projects early. A missed '100' declaration can cost you the entire game.
If you are the contractor and have only 1 trump, don't bid Hokom; the Khosara penalty is too high.

variations.name: Kahwa Variation
variations.description: Includes more detailed doubling rules where the score can be multiplied up to four times.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Kahwa rules change how doubling and Gahwa multiply scores, but those numeric multipliers are not yet modeled as structured engine overrides.

scoring.description: Points are calculated after all tricks are played. Card points: in Hokom trump J=20, 9=14, A=11, 10=10, K=4, Q=3, 8=0, 7=0; non-trump A=11, 10=10, K=4, Q=3, J=2, 9=0, 8=0, 7=0. Last trick adds 10. Total 162 (Hokom) or 130 (Sun). Convert to game points; first to 152 wins.

synthesis.shortDescription: Master the ultimate Saudi card game. Baloot is a rigorous test of memory, partnership, and strategic bidding. Whether you're aiming for a '100' project or managing a 'Locked' game, every trick counts double in the race to 152.
